Costa Rica Implements Sweeping Tariffs Amid Trade Dispute, Economy Feels Strain

SAN JOSÉ, June 14—Costa Rica’s government has imposed broad tariffs on a wide range of imported goods, citing an ongoing trade dispute with several key trading partners, officials confirmed Friday. The move, which took effect earlier this week, has already begun to disrupt commerce and raise concerns among businesses and consumers.

The Ministry of Economy, Industry, and Commerce announced tariffs of up to 25% on products spanning electronics, textiles, machinery, and processed foods. The measure, described as temporary, responds to what officials called “unfair trade practices” by foreign exporters.

“We cannot allow our domestic industries to be undermined,” Vice Minister Laura Rojas said at a press briefing. “These tariffs are necessary to level the playing field while negotiations continue.”

Retailers and importers say the new tariffs are having immediate effects. “We’re seeing wholesale prices jump overnight,” said Esteban Navarro, manager of the commercial group Gama Uno. “If this continues, consumers will face higher prices for basic goods and electronics within days.”

The Costa Rican Chamber of Industries warned that local manufacturers relying on imported inputs may also be hit. “Our supply chains are deeply integrated with foreign markets,” said Chamber President Rodrigo Pacheco. “Prolonged tariffs could slow production and threaten jobs.”

Economists estimate the tariffs could increase inflation by up to 1.5 percentage points if they remain in place for several months. The government has not specified a timeline for lifting the measures, stating only that talks with trade partners are ongoing.

Port officials reported a slowdown in container traffic at Puerto Limón, with some shipments delayed as importers reconsider logistics.
